title: POST Requests
subtitle: Sending data — JSON body, Content-Type, and handling the response
author: KERNAL Team

whyItExists.problem: GET requests only send data in the URL (query params and path params). Sending structured data (a user object, a form submission, a new post) requires a request body.
whyItExists.solution: POST, PUT, and PATCH requests can include a body — a payload sent to the server. For APIs, this is usually JSON: set Content-Type: application/json and stringify your data with JSON.stringify(). The server parses it and uses it to create or update resources.
whyItExists.whenToUse: Creating resources (POST), fully replacing a resource (PUT), partially updating a resource (PATCH).
whyItExists.whenNotToUse: Don't use POST for reads (use GET). Don't put sensitive data in GET query params — it appears in server logs and browser history.

explainModes.beginner: To send data with fetch(), add method: 'POST', headers: { 'Content-Type': 'application/json' }, and body: JSON.stringify(yourData). The Content-Type header tells the server that the body is JSON. JSON.stringify converts your JavaScript object to a JSON string for sending.
explainModes.simple: fetch(url, { method: 'POST', headers: { 'Content-Type': 'application/json' }, body: JSON.stringify(data) }). For PUT: same but include the full object. For PATCH: same but include only the changed fields. For DELETE: usually no body — fetch(url, { method: 'DELETE' }). Response: check res.ok, then res.json() for the created/updated record. 201 Created for POST, 200 OK for PUT/PATCH, 204 No Content for DELETE.
explainModes.standard: Content-Type header: required for POST/PUT/PATCH with a body. application/json for JSON data. application/x-www-form-urlencoded for HTML form data. multipart/form-data for file uploads (use FormData object, not JSON.stringify). Forgetting Content-Type: many servers treat the body as a string and don't parse it — you'll get empty req.body. Accept header: tells the server what format you want in response — usually application/json. Request body encoding: fetch() body can be a string, Blob, BufferSource, FormData, URLSearchParams, or ReadableStream.
explainModes.technical: JSON.stringify edge cases: Date objects → ISO strings. undefined values → omitted. Functions → omitted. Circular references → throws. JSON.stringify(data, null, 2) for pretty printing (useful for debugging). For large objects, JSON.stringify is synchronous and blocks the thread — consider structuredClone() + worker for huge payloads. Sending binary data: pass a Blob or ArrayBuffer as body — no Content-Type needed (browser infers). Server-sent Content-Length: some servers require it — add headers: { 'Content-Length': body.length } for compatibility.
explainModes.deepDive: Idempotency keys for POST: many payment APIs use an Idempotency-Key header. The server stores this key and returns the same response if it sees it again — safe to retry POST without creating duplicates. Optimistic locking: APIs use ETag header (a hash of the current version). You send If-Match: <etag> with PUT/PATCH. If the resource changed since you read it, the server returns 412 Precondition Failed — prevents overwriting someone else's changes. Request compression: send Content-Encoding: gzip and compress the body — useful for large JSON payloads over slow networks.

questions.question: What happens if you send a POST request with a JSON body but forget to set the Content-Type: application/json header?
options: fetch() throws a TypeError before sending the request
The server receives the JSON string but may not parse it as JSON — it depends on the server. Many frameworks (Express without express.json()) will give you an empty req.body.
The browser automatically adds Content-Type based on the body type
The server always rejects the request with 415 Unsupported Media Type
questions.explanation: Without Content-Type, the server doesn't know how to interpret the body. Some servers default to text/plain and return the raw string as req.body. Express with express.json() only parses bodies where Content-Type is application/json — without it, req.body is undefined. Always set Content-Type: 'application/json' when sending JSON. Some servers return 415 Unsupported Media Type, others just ignore the body — behavior varies, so always set the header.

faq.q: Do I always need Content-Type for POST requests?
faq.a: For JSON bodies, yes — always set Content-Type: 'application/json'. For FormData (file uploads), do NOT set Content-Type manually — the browser sets it automatically with the correct multipart boundary. For URLSearchParams (form encoding), the browser also sets the correct Content-Type automatically. The rule: only set Content-Type manually for JSON (application/json) and raw text bodies.
